paragraphs.text: Now he distinctly shows what subjects owe to their magistrates, that is, obedience: from which he shows that no man is free: and the obedience we owe is such that it is not only due to the highest magistrate himself, but also even to the lowest, who has any office under him.
Indeed, though an apostle, though an evangelist, though a prophet; Chrysostom. Therefore the tyranny of the pope over all kingdoms must be thrown down to the ground.

paragraphs.text: A reason taken from the nature of the thing itself: for to what purpose are they placed in higher degree, but in order that the inferiors should be subject to them?

Another argument of great force: because God is author of this order: so that those who are rebels ought to know that they make war with God himself: and because of this they purchase for themselves great misery and calamity.

paragraphs.text: The third argument, taken from the reason for which they were made, which is that they are to be most profitable: because God by this means preserves the good and bridles the wicked: by which words the magistrates themselves are put in mind of that duty which they owe to their subjects.

paragraphs.text: The conclusion: we must obey the magistrate, not only for fear of punishment, but much more because (although the magistrate has no power over the conscience of man, yet seeing he is God's minister) he cannot be resisted by any good conscience.
paragraphs.anchor: Wherefore ye must needs be subject

paragraphs.text: So far as we lawfully may: for if unlawful things are commanded to us, we must answer as Peter teaches us, "It is better to obey God than men."
paragraphs.label: d

paragraphs.text: He sums up the main thing, in which consists the obedience of subjects.
paragraphs.anchor: For this cause pay ye tribute

paragraphs.text: Obedience, and that from the heart.
paragraphs.label: e

paragraphs.text: Reverence, which (as we have reason) we must give to the magistrate.
paragraphs.label: f

paragraphs.text: He shows how very few judgments need to be executed, that is, if we so order our life as no man may justly require anything from us, besides only that which we owe one to another, by the perpetual law of charity.
He commends charity as a concise statement of the whole law.
paragraphs.anchor: for he that loveth another hath

paragraphs.text: Has not only done one commandment, but performed generally that which the law commands.
paragraphs.label: g

paragraphs.text: For the whole law commands nothing else but that we love God and our neighbour. But seeing that Paul speaks here of the duties we owe one to another, we must restrain this word "law" to the second table of the ten commandments.
paragraphs.label: h

paragraphs.text: An application taken from the circumstances of the time: which also itself puts us in mind of our duty, seeing that this remains, after which the darkness of ignorance and wicked affections by the knowledge of God's truth is driven out of us, that we order our life according to that certain and sure rule of all righteousness and honesty, being fully grounded upon the power of the Spirit of Christ.
In other places we are said to be in the light, but yet so that it does not yet appear what we are, for as yet we see but as it were in the twilight.
paragraphs.label: i

paragraphs.text: That kind of life which those lead that flee the light.
